home.eyebrow: Web applications developed for basic thermodynamics courses at the Department of Physics, Lund University, Sweden
home.description: A collection of simple, presentation-ready thermodynamics simulations for lectures and self-study. Explore temperature, heat flow, engines, entropy, and state variables with visual tools built for classroom intuition.
home.developmentNotice: These simulations are works in progress.
home.bugReportLink: Bug reports and feedback are welcome.

stirlingIllustration.title: Stirling Engine Illustration
stirlingIllustration.description: Explore an ideal Stirling cycle with helium. The pV diagram, calculations, and engine model are synchronized.
stirlingIllustration.diagramLabel: pV diagram for an ideal Stirling cycle
stirlingIllustration.engineLabel: Cutaway model of a Stirling engine with regenerator, cylinder, pistons, and flywheel

controls.manualHint: Drag around the flywheel to turn the cycle in either direction. Release and grab again as needed, or use the angle slider. Start resumes automatic motion.

engine.idealNote: Ideal cycle: cam-controlled dwells; perfect regeneration. Rod volume and matrix pore volume neglected.

processBuilder.title: Circuit Processes
processBuilder.description: Build a pV process diagram by placing isotherms, adiabats, isochores, and isobars. Snap endpoints together to create numbered states.
processBuilder.instructions: Double-click a process to add it, or drag it onto the diagram.
processBuilder.emptyTable: Add state changes to start entering values.

errors.noProcesses: Add at least one state change before solving.
errors.inconsistent: The entered values are overspecified or inconsistent.
errors.underdetermined: The entered values are underspecified. Add more known p, V, T, mass, or molar amount values.
errors.splitState: The entered value is inconsistent with the connected state changes and would split a numbered state.
errors.maxProcesses: The diagram can contain at most six state changes.

warnings.temperatureDof: The state temperatures span {min}–{max} K. For this gas, the fixed degrees of freedom model is only a rough approximation outside about {low}–{high} K.

help.stateChanges: Double-click or drag a process into the pV diagram. Endpoints snap into numbered states; use Erase state change and click a line, endpoint, or state marker to remove it.
help.values: Values in bold are manual inputs and are kept as constraints. Values not in bold have been calculated. The button Calculate fills in missing values; Recalculate replaces calculated values based on the bold manual ones.
help.gasModel: Choose units and working gas here. Mass and amount also become bold manual constraints when typed; if one is calculated, Recalculate may replace it.
help.energy: Heat and work are calculated from the current state changes and state values. For an ideal Stirling cycle, the extra boxes assume perfect regeneration, so the isochoric heat flows are recovered internally.

energy.title: Calculated heat and work
energy.empty: Add state changes and state values to calculate heat and work.
energy.stirlingRegeneratorNote: Ideal Stirling cycle with perfect regeneration: the isochoric heat flows are internally recovered.

heatTemperature.title: Gas, heat and temperature
heatTemperature.description: Heat a gas. Move its piston. Discover what changes—and where the energy goes.
heatTemperature.stateSpace: The same state, on a graph
heatTemperature.lockedQuestion: Where does the heat go if the gas cannot expand?
heatTemperature.lockedExplanation: Volume stays fixed. All added heat increases internal energy: temperature and pressure rise.
heatTemperature.loadedQuestion: Why does the same heat produce a smaller temperature rise than during isochoric heating?
heatTemperature.loadedExplanation: The gas expands against a fixed external pressure. Added heat both warms the gas and does work.
heatTemperature.insulatedQuestion: Can temperature rise without adding heat?
heatTemperature.insulatedExplanation: Compress or expand the insulated gas. Work done on it is taken from or added to its internal energy, even though Q = 0.
heatTemperature.particleNote: Particles are illustrative. Their speed scales with √T; their number stays fixed.
heatTemperature.heatControl: Net heat added from the starting state
heatTemperature.energyTitle: Follow the energy · Q = W + ΔU
heatTemperature.heat: Heat added to the gas · Q
heatTemperature.work: Work done by the gas · W
heatTemperature.internal: Internal energy of the gas · ΔU
heatTemperature.signNote: Values are changes compared to the starting state. W > 0 is work done by the gas during expansion; Q > 0 is heat entering the gas. Bar lengths show magnitudes.
heatTemperature.graphNote: The filled circle shows the current state. The open circle is the initial state. The grey line shows the allowed path of the process.
heatTemperature.surfaceNote: Every point on the mesh satisfies pV = nRT. Coloured lines are isotherms; the dark path follows your experiment.
heatTemperature.modelNote: 0.040 mol of a monatomic ideal gas, initially at 300 K and 1.00 l (about 1.00 bar). Quasistatic motion; friction and heat losses neglected. Cv = 3R/2, Cp = 5R/2, γ = 5/3. Insulated motion obeys TV^(γ−1) = constant. Each experiment starts from the same state. The slider sets net heat or volume; it is not a heater-power control. Isothermal motion is held at 300 K by a thermal reservoir: Q = W = nRT ln(V/V₀), ΔU = 0.
heatTemperature.isothermalQuestion: Can a gas expand without cooling down?
heatTemperature.isothermalExplanation: A temperature-controlled water bath keeps T = 300 K. During expansion heat enters; during compression heat leaves. The internal energy stays constant: Q = W.
